text: The ACM A. M. Turing Award is an annual honor bestowed by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) for significant and enduring technical contributions to computer science. It is widely regarded as the highest achievement in the field and is commonly known as the "Nobel Prize of Computing." As of 2025, 79 individuals have received the award, with Andrew Barto and Richard S. Sutton being the most recent recipients, awarded in 2024. The award is named after Alan Turing, often called the "Father of Computer Science," a British mathematician and former reader in mathematics at the University of Manchester. Turing is credited as the founder of theoretical computer science and artificial intelligence and played a crucial role in the Allied decryption of the Enigma cipher during World War II. From 2007 to 2013, the award included a US$250,000 prize, funded by Intel and Google. Since 2014, the prize has been US$1 million, also supported by Google. The first recipient was Alan Perlis in 1966. Donald Knuth was the youngest recipient, winning in 1974 at age 36, while Alfred Aho was the oldest, receiving it in 2020 at age 79. Only three women have been awarded the prize: Frances Allen in 2006, Barbara Liskov in 2008, and Shafi Goldwasser in 2012.
